1edcdbb14ddd6ae6: JAKARTA: Indonesia's president railed Wednesday against "countries that like to insult" his nation over wildfires that have razed vast areas, spewing toxic haze into neighbouring countries.

The Southeast Asian giant has for months struggled to contain fires that Nusantara Atlas, an independent monitor analysing satellite data, said have consumed more than 1.9 million hectares in the nine months to September.

The haze has sent air pollution levels surging to dangerous levels not only at home, but also in Malaysia, Singapore and East Timor, prompting the Asean regional bloc to call a meeting over the crisis.

"As for certain countries that like to insult the Indonesian nation, when the time comes, we will reveal the companies involved" Prabowo told a cabinet meeting Wednesday, claiming that "many corporations bear responsibility" for the crisis.
He did not name names or nationalities.
The leaders of Indonesia's neighbours have offered help while steering clear of overt criticism at the highest diplomatic level.
With public anger growing, however, a Malaysian MP last week called for Indonesia to be treated as an "outcast" in the region.
"Indonesia is a polite and patient nation. Our country is often insulted, but believe me, our nation does not want to be insulted all the time," Prabowo said.
The president said he had asked for investigations into the cause of the fires which he insisted was "not purely natural."
Experts say Indonesia's wildfires can be blamed in large part on slash-and-burn land-clearing practices that result in the destruction of fire-resistant forest cover and drained peatlands.
This year, the blazes were intensified by a severe drought fuelled by the El Nino weather phenomenon.
"I am asking the police, the Attorney General's Office, the Ministry of Forestry, with the support of the Armed Forces and intelligence services, to investigate," said Prabowo.
"The people have also caught various individuals who deliberately set fires – this is something we can regard as environmental terrorism."

The president, who marked two years in office Tuesday with record-low approval levels, said deliberate fire-setting amounted to "a crime against humanity, because what they have done endangers the health of millions of our citizens."
Once the evidence is in, he added, "we will revoke all licenses of companies that violate the law."--AFP

db0629be998ab349: KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysia ended their IBF World Cup campaign with two hard-earned team bronze medals after both national quartets narrowly missed out on the finals in Munich, Germany, today.

The defending men's champions fell 3-2 to Australia, while the women's team suffered an equally heartbreaking 3-2 defeat to arch-rivals Singapore, with both semi-final encounters going down to the deciding fifth game.
Despite missing out on gold, Malaysia could take pride in being one of only two nations, alongside the United States, to reach the semi-finals in both team events.
The double bronze brought Malaysia's medal haul to three, following Natasha Roslan's silver in the women's singles on Sunday.
Malaysian Tenpin Bowling Congress (MTBC) secretary-general Maradona Chok said there was plenty to be proud of despite the disappointment.

"Of course, we wanted to go all the way, especially with both teams reaching the semi-finals. But to come away with three medals and have both our teams among the world's top four is still a very encouraging achievement," said Maradona.
The men's quartet of Rafiq Ismail, Timmy Tan, Tun Hakim Tun Hasnul Azam and Ahmad Muaz Fishol came agonisingly close to defending the historic crown they captured in Hong Kong last year.
They made a strong start against Australia, winning the opening game 224-192 before their opponents drew level with a 206-175 victory.
Malaysia regained the advantage by taking the third 217-164, but the Australians responded 195-168 before producing a commanding 275-194 in the decider.
Despite relinquishing their crown, the quartet could take heart from an impressive recovery after winning just two of their opening six qualifying matches.
They reeled off five consecutive victories to reach the knockout stage before defeating Qatar 3-1 in the last 16 and Canada 3-2 in the quarter-finals.

"The boys deserve a lot of credit. They had a difficult start, but showed tremendous character to fight their way back and reach the semi-finals. They gave everything they had in trying to defend the title," said Maradona.
The women's quartet of Natasha, Sin Li Jane, Adelia Nur Irwan Syazalee and Nur Hazirah Ramli also showed tremendous resilience in their semi-final against Singapore.
Trailing 2-0 after losing the opening games 236-203, 211-200, the Malaysians fought back superbly to win the next two 259-215, 194-180.
However, Singapore held their nerve to clinch the decider 191-174, denying Malaysia a second consecutive women's team final appearance.
Earlier, the national women had survived another five-game thriller to beat Australia 3-2 in the last 16 before sweeping aside Greece 3-0 in the quarter-finals.

"The girls showed great determination too. Coming back from two games down against Singapore says a lot about their fighting spirit. It was disappointing to fall just short, but they can hold their heads high," said Maradona.
Interestingly, even the US, boasting a formidable line-up of Professional Bowlers Association (PBA) and Professional Women's Bowling Association (PWBA) Tour stars, missed out on both finals.
Their men's team lost 3-1 to France, while the women fell 3-2 to Denmark.
Malaysia had enjoyed a historic campaign at last year's World Cup in Hong Kong, returning with two golds and two silvers.
Natasha captured the women's singles crown, while the men's quartet claimed a maiden team gold. Rafiq added a men's singles silver, with the women's team also finishing runners-up.

612a6fdef38d2fa8: PONTIANAK: Residents of Indonesian Borneo urged the government on Wednesday to do more to combat the wildfires consuming vast tracts of land and emitting a foul haze that has sickened thousands and curtailed daily life for months.
They spoke out as a court in Pontianak, West Kalimantan, began hearing arguments into the admissibility of a case brought against the state by residents in the province of nearly six million people.

"The issue... is not merely about burning forests and land, it is also closely tied to public health, air quality, economic activity, education and the safety of residents," resident Achmad Mundzirin told AFP in Pontianak.
"This lawsuit serves as a means to demand that the government be held accountable for its handling of forest and land fires," the 36-year-old said.
Lawyers have filed a class action case claiming "negligence, omission and failure" on the part of the government that has resulted in "a massive public health crisis" in West Kalimantan.
It singles out President Prabowo Subianto and 26 officials from the national, provincial and local government, as well as police and emergency services.
Glorio Sanen, a lawyer for the plaintiffs, told reporters on Wednesday the community was suffering.
"The president must directly lead the handling of this smoke disaster so that our aspirations, our hope for fresh air, blue skies and sunshine can return here in West Kalimantan," he said.
The government has deployed firefighters assisted by volunteers across affected areas, and used cloud-seeding and water-bombing with mixed success.
Experts say Indonesia's wildfires can be blamed in large part on slash-and-burn land-clearing practices that result in the destruction of fire-resistant forest cover and drained peatlands.
This year, the blazes have been intensified by a severe drought fuelled by the El Nino weather phenomenon.
The plaintiffs insist the government could have done more in preparation – drilling more borewells and distributing sufficient firefighting equipment.

They want the government to declare a national emergency to release resources and are suing for free health care and compensation for the families of people who died of fire-related respiratory ailments.
Rokman Torang, a lawyer for the state, insisted on Wednesday that the national and provincial governments "have already responded to this haze issue."
Prabowo said Wednesday that "many corporations bear responsibility" for the fire and haze crisis, and vowed a thorough investigation.
For Pontianak resident Andi Fachrizal, 54, the court case held "important meaning for the environmental struggle."

"This legal process is a moment to reaffirm that the public's right to a good and healthy environment is not merely a norm enshrined in laws and regulations, but a right that must be protected and fulfilled by the state," he told AFP.--AFP

7a62ae7e6837745a: KUALA LUMPUR: Police have crippled an organised crime group known as Geng Suria, which was active in armed robberies across Kedah, following a special operation last month.

Federal Criminal Investigation Department director Datuk M Kumar S Muthuvelu said the integrated operation, conducted in collaboration with the Kedah police contingent's Criminal Investigation Department, was carried out in Kedah and Perak from Sept 24 to 27.
He said the group was led by a 30-year-old man and had nine members aged between 28 and 52.
"The group has been active since early 2024. Geng Suria has been linked to 20 property and violent crime cases involving armed gang robberies that caused injuries in Kedah.
"Police arrested six suspects aged between 28 and 39. All are being detained under the Security Offences (Special Measures) Act 2012 (SOSMA) until Oct 25, 2026," he said in a statement today.
The remaining three members are being held at Sungai Buloh Prison, Pokok Sena Prison and Sungai Petani Prison over various other criminal offences, he said.
Elaborating on the group's modus operandi, M Kumar said Geng Suria often targeted foreigners' homes, business premises and residential properties identified by its leader.
"During the robberies, group members used dangerous weapons such as knives and machetes and did not hesitate to injure victims to carry out their criminal activities.
"Their aggressive and violent actions caused fear and trauma among victims, some of whom sustained serious injuries in the attacks," he said.
He said the stolen goods were subsequently sold, with the proceeds distributed by the group leader according to each member's role.
"During the raids, police seized six mobile phones of various brands and 189 ecstasy pills weighing an estimated 101.12g.

"The drug seizure is being investigated under Section 39B of the Dangerous Drugs Act 1952. Checks also found that several suspects had previous records involving vehicle theft, housebreaking, drugs and gang robbery," he said.

M Kumar said police reports received since 2024 indicated that Geng Suria's activities had caused losses amounting to hundreds of thousands of ringgit, while creating fear and threatening victims' safety.
He said the Attorney-General's Chambers had agreed to charge all nine alleged group members under Section 130V(1) of the Penal Code for being members of an organised criminal group.
"The 9 Geng Suria members will be charged tomorrow, Oct 22, 2026, at the Sungai Petani Sessions Court in Kedah," he said.

e2dc8fe273ba5067: ANKARA: Turkiye, Qatar, Pakistan, and Indonesia signed an agreement on Wednesday to boost defence cooperation and strengthen defensive capabilities, the Turkish Defence Ministry said.
In a statement, the ministry said the countries signed the "Badr Memorandum of Understanding" in Doha as a sign of their desire to further deepen cooperation and develop partnerships.

"The agreement holds substantial economic importance," it said, adding the accord sought to foster cooperation in military production, boost military capabilities, and help collaboration in technical military training, research and development.

"By leveraging the unique military production capabilities of each country, the initiative will facilitate cooperation and integration, enhance defence industrial capacities, and enable the fulfillment of the needs of allied and friendly nations," it added.
Turkiye, which has Nato's second-largest army and a robust defence industry, has been helping Gulf nations, including Qatar, where it has a military base, bolster their defences amid the Iran war.

In August, it signed a mutual defence pact with nuclear-armed Pakistan and Saudi Arabia, under which an attack on one party constitutes an attack on all. Ankara also has close ties with Indonesia, notably in the defence industry.
The ministry said the Badr accord would strengthen ties between the countries' defence industries and bolster collaboration to promote security and achieve shared objectives.
Haluk Gorgun, the chairman of Turkiye's Defence Industry Presidency, said the accord formed the foundation of a "strategic cooperation" to develop joint production and technology.

"Technology sharing, joint development and strengthening domestic production capabilities lie at the heart of sustainable defence industry. As Turkiye, we value partnerships that go beyond off-the-shelf procurement models, that foster the development of a nation's own human capital and industrial infrastructure," Gorgun said in a statement.

"We believe that the Badr Memorandum of Understanding will contribute to transforming the complementary capabilities of Qatar, Pakistan, Indonesia, and Turkiye into concrete projects," he added.--REUTERS

22142f8e91cd1525: Microsoft is raising OneDrive's supported macOS sync limit to one million items, matching Windows, alongside new Copilot features, sharing controls, and an admin command-line tool.

The macOS preview is scheduled for the Insiders ring this month, with general availability targeted for June 2027. Eligible devices must meet hardware and configuration requirements; others retain the existing 300,000-item supported limit.
"This increase is intended to help organizations with large OneDrive and SharePoint libraries sync more content reliably across devices," Microsoft said.

However, sync performance may suffer for large numbers of read-only files or accounts under legal hold. "We are actively working to improve performance and reliability for these scenarios," Microsoft said.
Microsoft's cull of OneDrive's File Explorer shortcuts wasn't a retreat from AI. Its latest announcement gives Copilot more to do.

The assistant can now be asked to analyze across files (for example, selecting several spreadsheets and getting the bot to come up with charts and graphs), told to organize folders, or save a repeated workflow as a personal skill in a Markdown file. There is also a Prompt Gallery to save the user from having to come up with their own ideas.

Perhaps most interesting is the addition of "Hero Links," designed to end the proliferation of links to files and folders in OneDrive as permission needs change. The feature provides one link per file and folder by default, with permissions that can be updated while keeping the same URL.
Automatic expiration controls are still coming, however. Organizations that require time-limited access will want to check that gap before adopting the feature.

Administrators also get a OneDrive Sync command-line tool, available in private preview, for inspecting accounts, configuration, policies, and sync status. The tool can pull information from the OneDrive sync client and provide data on status, policy troubleshooting, and issue diagnosis, from folder backup and policy problems on a single PC to identifying devices that need attention across an organization.
And yes, there is, of course, integration with AI agents. ®

d7527620a046d8d7: ATHENS: Thousands of students and teachers took to the streets across Greece on Wednesday, demanding higher state funding for education, better facilities and less-crowded classrooms, echoing protesters in other European countries.

About 10,000 demonstrators, including school and university students, rallied peacefully in central Athens and suburbs, police said. Others joined rallies in cities across the country, all voicing their solidarity with growing protests in France and elsewhere in Europe over soaring living costs and over what they called crumbling school conditions.

The protests add pressure on prime minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis' centre-right government, which faces elections in mid-2027, as Greeks struggle with stagnant wages, high rents and rising energy costs years after the country's debt crisis.

"From Greece to France, we want public, free education," protesters chanted as they gathered outside parliament. Students had set up tents in central Athens' Syntagma Square and staged an overnight protest before Wednesday's march.
State school and hospital operations were disrupted as some primary school teachers and doctors walked out, protesting over pay and staff shortages.

Education Minister Sofia Zacharaki said before the protests that she was hearing students' demands. She acknowledged housing costs were putting pressure on Greek households and said projects worth more than €733 million (US$823 million) were underway for new student residences and facilities upgrades.

Greece has recovered from a 2009-2018 debt crisis, when wages and education spending were cut under austerity in exchange for three international bailouts worth about €290 billion. Salaries have increased since, but real purchasing power for many Greeks is still among the lowest in the EU and has taken a fresh blow from rising inflation and soaring fuel prices linked to the Iran war.
The average monthly salary of €1,500 (US$1,685) remains stuck at the 2009 level, and many young Greeks have been priced out of housing in cities by skyrocketing rents.

"Surviving here is very difficult, the rent is really high, and the houses are really small. Our parents can’t make ends meet to pay for our rent, the electricity, for our life here," said university student Georgia Foukidou, 21, who joined the protest in Athens.
The demonstrations follow days of protests in France and Albania, where anger over rising living costs and perceived corruption has led to clashes and heavy property damage.

Protests in Greece have been largely peaceful in recent months. Mitsotakis' government has said state subsidies and other aid to prop up households and businesses against rising energy costs would reach about €1 billion.
fb9b192333f438c2: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 21 — Authorities should examine how much ship emissions contribute to air pollution around major ports, particularly during haze episodes originating from Indonesia, says maritime industry expert Datuk Seri Jeyenderan M. Ramasamy.

Jeyenderan, the chief executive officer of Maritime Network Sdn Bhd, said Malaysia’s strategic location along the Strait of Malacca, one of the world’s busiest shipping lanes, offered significant opportunities to develop its marine fuel supply sector, but environmental considerations should not be overlooked.

“As more vessels pass through our waters, we should ensure that ship emissions are properly monitored and that our ports develop sustainably. The environmental impact of shipping activity deserves closer attention, particularly when transboundary haze affects Malaysia,” he said in a statement.
He said Port Klang and ports in Johor were strategically positioned along international shipping routes, giving Malaysia the opportunity to attract more vessels to bunker locally.

However, ships burning heavy fuel oil, including high-sulphur fuel oil (HSFO), can release air pollutants such as sulphur oxides, particulate matter and other combustion-related pollutants, depending on the fuel used and engine operating conditions.
The International Maritime Organization (IMO) introduced a global sulphur limit of 0.50 per cent by mass for fuel used by ships outside designated emission control areas from January 1, 2020.

Ships may use higher-sulphur fuel if they operate under the applicable rules with an approved exhaust gas cleaning system, commonly called a scrubber. The limit for fuel used on board is separate from the rules governing HSFO carried as cargo.

Jeyenderan said the relevant authorities could consider monitoring air quality around major ports, checking compliance with marine fuel sulphur limits and studying pollution levels during haze episodes to better understand the contribution of different sources.

He stressed that reliable monitoring data would help policymakers distinguish between pollution from transboundary haze and emissions from local sources, including shipping, while supporting efforts to balance the maritime industry’s growth with environmental protection.

Echoing the call, Universiti Malaysia Terengganu adjunct professor Nazery Khalid urged the authorities to closely monitor ship emissions during haze episodes, saying Malaysia’s efforts to attract more vessels and expand seaborne trade should not come at the expense of meeting its emissions targets and its international commitments to combat climate change.

“As a responsible maritime nation and a long-standing member of the International Maritime Organization Council, Malaysia is duty-bound to ensure maritime operations in its waters are carried out in an eco-friendly manner, in full adherence to national laws and international standards.

“By ensuring emissions from shipping activities are closely monitored, even during the haze, Malaysia can also underscore its commitment to meeting its net-zero target by 2050. Shipping, which facilitates close to 90 per cent of its trade, and the maritime industry in general can play a leading role in realising this national agenda by operating sustainably,” said Nazery in the joint statement.

00c0289996c374cc: ISTANBUL, Oct 21 — US researchers have developed an artificial intelligence tool that can predict cancer patients’ survival chances from a single facial photograph, according to a study published Monday in the journal The Lancet Digital Health, Anadolu Ajansi reported.

Developed by researchers at Mass General Brigham in the US state of Massachusetts, the system, called FAHR-Face, analyses facial features to estimate biological age and mortality risk, potentially helping doctors make treatment decisions.

The model was trained on more than 40 million facial photos and adapted into two tools: FAHR-FaceAge, which estimates biological age, and FAHR-FaceSurvival, which predicts cancer patients’ survival directly from facial images without relying on age estimates.

Researchers found that the survival model focused mainly on areas beneath the eyes and around the nose, while the age-estimation model examined facial features around the mouth and temples, suggesting the two systems identify different health-related patterns.
The survival model was trained on images of 34,363 patients and tested on another 3,820, with results independently validated using data from 4,892 cancer patients in the Netherlands.
Researchers found that patients classified in the highest-risk group had more than three times the mortality risk of those in the lowest-risk group, even after accounting for clinical factors.

Patients whose faces appeared at least five years older than their actual age also had a 21 per cent higher mortality risk, while those appearing at least five years younger had a 17 per cent lower risk.
Combining the two models further improved the accuracy of survival predictions, according to the study.

Researchers said the technology could help doctors assess patients’ health and guide treatment decisions, although further validation is needed before it can be widely used in clinical practice. — Bernama-Anadolu
ff022620b2ebf6ca: ALLAGASH (US), Oct 21 — Early snow is already dusting the north-easternmost US state of Maine, where a canny 73-year-old Republican senator is having to run the race of her life to help save Donald Trump’s party from being frozen out of power nationwide.
Susan Collins has held her Senate seat for three decades, becoming a near immovable fixture in the state’s political landscape.

But with President Trump deeply unpopular nationwide and Mainers furious about surging fuel prices ahead of winter, Collins’s Democratic challenger is eying an upset — and a chance to make his party’s outside bid to regain the Senate a reality.
The stakes are enormous in the race between Collins and logger-turned-politician Troy Jackson, as Maine is crucial for any Democratic path to a US Senate majority.

While Democrats are forecast to win the House of Representatives in the November 3 midterms, they would need to clinch the Senate too if they want to stop Trump’s right-wing agenda in its tracks, including his power to nominate Supreme Court justices.
Time for change?
About one-third of Maine’s voters are unaffiliated with either party. Because independents generally are opposed to Trump nationwide, that could work to Jackson’s advantage.
Most voters interviewed by AFP agreed that Collins had done well in funneling federal funding back to Maine over the years and that 58-year-old newcomer Jackson would not be so successful.

But like many Mainers, retired teacher Louisa Beckett believes a perfect storm of national setbacks — cost-of-living hikes, the Iran war, and allegations of massive Trump corruption — could finally sink Collins.
“She does a lot for the state of Maine,” Beckett said while attending a “No Kings” anti-Trump rally.
“However this is much, much bigger than the state of Maine,” added the 80-year-old. “It’s about our democracy, it’s about our Constitution.”
Divided communities
Both Collins and Jackson hail from the same sparsely populated, heavily forested northern county of Aroostook, bordering Canada.
Logging, hunting and cross-border trade are the focuses there — but these days, so is politics and the price of fuel.
Fiery arguments have broken out among patrons at Rock’s Family Diner in the Aroostook frontier town of Fort Kent.
The divisions are even visible in Jackson’s remote hometown of Allagash, where red Collins signs are visible outside some houses in the community of 227 people.
Hilton Hafford, 68, said he was all for his local friend Jackson, but added with a grimace: “My sisters and brother are on the other side.”
A retired logger who guides moose hunts, Hafford said Jackson will be the best to push back against Trump in Washington.
But Collins’s main pitch is that despite being a Republican she has already proven sufficiently independent from Trump’s most extreme policies.

“The most remarkable thing she manages to do is to insulate herself from the unpopularity of a president in the same political party,” University of Southern Maine political science professor Ron Schmidt told AFP.
“Even the (Mainers) who aren’t crazy about her have a certain amount of ‘the devil you know is better than the devil you don’t’ attitude towards her.”
And yet some experts believe Collins is deeply vulnerable, with diesel and heating oil prices soaring.
Maine is America’s most heating oil-dependent state, and residents expressed outrage at how fixed-income households could suffer this winter.
‘Hardcore Democrat’ for Collins
Maine has not backed a Republican presidential candidate since 1988, but it’s far from a Democratic stronghold, with voters regularly choosing Republicans for Congress.
In Collins’s hometown of Caribou, brewery owner and Collins supporter Shawn Pelletier said the senator does face “a lot of headwind.”
But Collins retains considerable loyalty from across society.
“My father is a hardcore Democrat, and he has a Susan Collins sign on his lawn,” Pelletier said.

Part of the appeal, said Brandon Lane, a 37-year-old who runs outdoor adventures company Allagash Guide Service, is that Collins exerts her power in Washington to help Maine, including negotiating exemptions on Canadian goods like road salt.
“With Susan Collins, you know what you’re getting,” he told AFP.
Polls show the candidates mostly neck and neck. Yet Maine is notoriously hard to poll accurately — and Collins is a survivor.
In 2020 she trailed her Democratic challenger in pre-election polling. Then she won by nine points. — AFP

‘Not a Trump person’

<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

United Auto Workers union member Rob Banks walks between homes to promote the union’s preferred slate of candidates for the upcoming midterm elections in Warren, Michigan, on October 10, 2026. — AFP pic

2ae0d3b75b3c2ee5: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 21 — Matcha, a powdered Japanese green tea that once dominated the beverage scene, particularly at trendy cafes before making its way to roadside stalls, is now gaining wider popularity in the culinary industry.
No longer confined to lattes, fancy drinks and desserts, matcha is increasingly being incorporated into a variety of savoury dishes, including nasi lemak, burgers and even fried catfish.
While such combinations may sound unusual, they have found their own following, with some consumers embracing the notion that “the greener, the healthier”.

But does this growing trend of matcha-infused dishes represent creative culinary innovation and a healthier way of eating, or is it simply a marketing strategy to attract attention and gain popularity on social media?
Innovation or healthy eating?

Senior lecturer at the Department of Science and Mathematics, Universiti Tun Hussein Onn Malaysia, Dr Adnin Afifi Nawi, views the current phenomenon primarily as a form of culinary creativity aimed at attracting customers.
He said that although matcha has antioxidant properties, various factors must be considered before labelling matcha-containing dishes as “healthy diet” options.

“If a food item goes viral because of its attractive colour or unique taste, there is nothing wrong with giving it a try. However, we should not immediately conclude that it is healthy simply because it contains matcha,” he told Bernama.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

No longer confined to lattes, fancy drinks and desserts, matcha is increasingly being incorporated into a variety of savoury dishes, including ‘nasi lemak’, burgers and even fried catfish. — Social media pic

Observing that consumer preferences have evolved, he said the elements of being “unique” and “visually appealing”, particularly when shared on social media, have become priorities among young people today.

“In the past, we chose food based on taste and quality, but purchasing behaviour has changed. Today, being ‘unique’ and ‘beautiful’ enough to post on TikTok or Instagram has become a priority. In the digital economy, consumer attention is a goldmine.
“The more unusual or extraordinary a dish is, the greater its potential to be shared and go viral.

“Matcha’s vibrant green colour makes it highly photogenic. If a food picture or video manages to captivate netizens within the first three seconds, the dish is likely to become highly sought after,” he said.
He added that international media had reported the growing global popularity of matcha, with demand for the ingredient outstripping supply.
“Reports by the South China Morning Post have also revealed that some traditional producers in Japan are struggling to meet surging global demand, fuelled by the influence of social media,” he said.
Understanding matcha

Explaining the health benefits of matcha from a scientific perspective, Professor Dr Norsham Juliana Nordin, an expert in chronophysiology and chrononutrition at the Faculty of Medicine and Health Sciences, Universiti Sains Islam Malaysia, said matcha is a powdered green tea derived from the Camellia sinensis plant and contains catechins, which are potent antioxidants.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Matcha’s vibrant green colour makes it highly photogenic. — AFP pic

Consuming foods containing catechins may help reduce inflammation in the body, boost metabolism, support weight management, and promote heart and blood vessel health. Matcha also has natural antibacterial and antiviral properties.
However, the nutrition expert stressed that the health value of a dish cannot be determined solely by the presence of a single ingredient considered beneficial.
Instead, she said, a balanced approach to healthy eating requires consideration of the overall composition of a meal, including portion size, preparation methods, frequency of consumption and timing.

“Matcha does have a sound nutritional basis because it contains polyphenols, particularly catechins such as epigallocatechin gallate (EGCG), as well as L-theanine and caffeine. Its use is therefore not merely a gimmick.
“However, when matcha is added to nasi lemak, burgers, noodles, traditional cakes or desserts, we cannot automatically assume that the entire dish has become a ‘health food’.

“The nutritional value is still determined by the overall dish. If only a small amount of matcha is added while the food remains high in calories, sugar, saturated fat or sodium, the overall nutritional impact does not change dramatically,” she told Bernama.
Matcha ‘nasi lemak’ and fried catfish

On viral food creations such as matcha nasi lemak and matcha-marinated fried catfish, Norsham Juliana said matcha has strong sensory appeal, with its green colour, umami flavour and slight bitterness lending dishes a premium image.
However, adding the ingredient to nasi lemak or fried catfish does not necessarily make either dish healthier.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

File picture showing bags of tea in a tea processing factory in Sayama, Japan. Excessive matcha consumption could cause caffeine-sensitive individuals to experience headaches, palpitations, restlessness and difficulty sleeping. — AFP pic

“For nasi lemak, the calorie, fat and sodium content, as well as portion size, still depend on the amount of coconut milk, sambal, anchovies and oil used, and how much is consumed. Adding matcha to the rice may contribute some polyphenols and introduce a variation in flavour and colour, but it does not ‘neutralise’ the coconut milk, salt or excess calories.

“A more meaningful way to make nasi lemak more balanced is to control portion size and the amount of coconut milk, oil and sodium used, while adding vegetables or cucumber. Choosing healthier cooking methods for the accompanying dishes would also help. Matcha can then be included as a creative addition.
“In other words, matcha may add value, but it is not a licence to disregard the nutritional composition of the entire meal,” she said.
The same applies to catfish prepared using matcha as a marinade.

She said matcha could contribute phenolic compounds, flavour and colour to the fish, but clinical evidence remains insufficient to claim that matcha-marinated catfish offers greater health benefits than conventionally prepared catfish.

“The greater difference to health usually comes from how the fish is cooked. Catfish marinated in matcha but deep-fried in large amounts of oil is still affected by the quantity of oil used, frying temperature, portion size and accompanying sauces.
“By contrast, grilled, baked or roasted fish prepared with controlled amounts of oil and salt generally has a better nutritional profile,” she explained.
At the same time, Norsham Juliana cautioned that exposing matcha to excessively high temperatures could reduce some of its beneficial properties.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

According to Professor Dr Norsham Juliana Nordin, an expert in chronophysiology and chrononutrition at the Faculty of Medicine and Health Sciences, Universiti Sains Islam Malaysia, high doses or the use of highly concentrated green tea extracts should not be regarded in the same way as ordinary food consumption. — AFP pic

“Catechins are not immune to heat. A study on matcha-enriched biscuits found that baking reduced the total catechin content by about 19 per cent compared with the dough. A bread study, meanwhile, showed that a substantial proportion of certain catechins could be retained after baking, although EGCG and epigallocatechin (EGC) were more susceptible to degradation than some other catechins,” she said.

“More precisely, cooking can reduce or alter some of matcha’s bioactive compounds, but it does not necessarily eliminate all of them. The higher the temperature and the longer the exposure, the greater the likelihood of changes occurring,” she added.
The risks of too much matcha
While enjoying matcha-infused dishes, consumers should also be aware of the potential risks associated with excessive consumption of foods containing the ingredient.

“Many people assume that ‘this cake contains matcha, so it must be healthier’, or that ‘this drink is green, so I can drink it frequently’. Another common mistake is overlooking the quantity consumed.

“In reality, the benefits and risks depend on the dose. A small serving is not the same as drinking several strong matcha beverages a day in addition to eating matcha desserts,” Norsham Juliana explained.
Citing the European Food Safety Authority, she said the consumption of 800 milligrammes or more of EGCG daily through food supplements had been associated with increased liver enzyme levels.

“High doses or the use of highly concentrated green tea extracts should not be regarded in the same way as ordinary food consumption. Safety assessments indicate that liver injury is rare, but particular attention is given to supplements or concentrated extracts containing high doses of EGCG, especially when taken as a large single dose,” she stressed.
She also advised consumers to consider matcha’s caffeine content and the timing of consumption, particularly those who are sensitive to caffeine.

“A third common mistake is overlooking timing. From the perspective of chrononutrition and chronophysiology, both what we consume and when we consume it matter. Drinking matcha in the morning has different implications for sleep compared with consuming a caffeinated matcha beverage late at night,” she said.
She added that excessive matcha consumption could cause caffeine-sensitive individuals to experience headaches, palpitations, restlessness and difficulty sleeping.
“There is nothing wrong with enjoying matcha, but do not eat with your eyes alone. Its green colour is appealing, but health cannot be judged by colour or a single ingredient.
“If you choose a matcha drink, reduce the amount of sugar and syrup. If you opt for matcha cake or pastries, remember that they are still desserts and keep your portions under control,” she advised.
She recommended that consumers practise moderation rather than blindly subscribing to the notion that “the greener, the healthier”. — Bernama
ab754bf975bbc756: GENEVA, Oct 21 — Non-communicable diseases account for three-quarters of deaths worldwide but affect different population groups in different ways, a World Health Organization study showed on Tuesday.

In its biggest-ever look at inequality in health and non-communicable diseases (NCDs), the WHO studied the top four killers — cancer, cardiovascular diseases, chronic respiratory diseases and diabetes.
It also looked at the five main risk factors driving them — tobacco use, alcohol consumption, obesity, unhealthy diets, physical inactivity and air pollution.

The report then scanned this across differences in NCD burden, prevention and care — by age, gender, economic status, education, place of residence, disability status, employment and migration status.
“This is the first effort to systematically measure inequalities in NCDs and their risk factors on a global scale,” said Ahmad Reza Hosseinpoor, who leads the WHO’s health inequality monitoring team.
“The findings show which populations are being left behind.”
NCDs cover eight of the top 10 causes of death, with cardiovascular diseases the biggest killer by far, claiming almost 20 million deaths a year.

The 10 years of national data, collected between 2013 and 2022, confirmed that socio-economic status influences health at every stage — from initial exposure to risk factors, through to diagnosis, treatment and disease management.
For example, the report found that in low- and middle-income countries, less educated populations suffered higher rates of hypertension and diabetes.
Cervical cancer screening rates are very low among the poorest and least-educated women; while tobacco use remains higher among less-educated men than among more educated men.
Looking at geographical factors, the study found that people in rural areas has significantly more limited access to hypertension diagnosis and cancer screening.
Gender and age also play a role. Men with hypertension are diagnosed and treated less frequently than women, even though they consume more tobacco and alcohol.
Conversely, obesity is more common among women, particularly in developing countries.
The study confirmed that social marginalisation, disability and migrant status were significant factors contributing to increased risk.
The United Nations’ health agency urged governments to raise health-related taxes on tobacco, alcohol and sugary drinks — measures that are particularly effective among low-income populations.
Countries were also encouraged to tailor insurance schemes or subsidies for under-served communities and to incorporate inequality indicators into their national health systems. — AFP

97d1409c4dcd2f73: Generative AI is saving open source developers time while giving maintainers more rubbish to sift through, according to a Linux Foundation survey.
Respondents estimated that a quarter of incoming pull requests – proposed code changes – were low-quality "AI slop."

Open source projects have spent the past year grappling with AI-generated contributions, useful vulnerability discoveries, false positives, and duplicate reports. Linus Torvalds has warmed to the tools, while remaining critical of low-quality submissions.
The foundation argues that projects need clearer policies and better tools to handle the influx.

Almost three-quarters (71 percent) of maintainers reckon GenAI has lowered the barriers to contributing to open source, but just over half (53 percent) disagree that the technology has improved community trust. Respondents estimated that AI cut code-authoring time by 52 percent on average. But for highly complex tasks, 21 percent reported taking longer.

Then there is governance. Only 35 percent of projects have a formal policy permitting GenAI use, while 32 percent have no policy and no plans for one, leaving expectations unclear across much of the community.

Hilary Carter, SVP of Research at the Linux Foundation, said: "Open source projects need to design for a growing AI-generated contributor base, not simply react to it. That means setting clear expectations for GenAI, putting responsibility for testing and disclosure on contributors and giving maintainers better tools to manage incoming pull requests."
Among large projects, the estimated share of incoming pull requests classified as AI slop rises to 31 percent.

The workload extends beyond proposed code changes. The curl project announced this week it will move low and medium severity severity flaws to public view to protect a security team almost overwhelmed by AI-assisted reports.
Project maintainer Daniel Stenberg said: "We are struggling as a project as all key maintainers feel strained, overloaded and brought to the brink of what we can muster."
On the need for better tools for maintainers, Carter said: "If we get those fundamentals right, AI can expand participation without overburdening and increasing costs for maintainers." ®

5173075304e6b98c: TOKYO, Oct 21 — Global exports of the rare earth yttrium have stalled, causing what a Japanese official described as a “supply-demand crunch”, with the Financial Times reporting that Tokyo was months away from running out of the critical metal.
Yttrium is essential for manufacturing consumer electronics, LEDs, aviation engines, semiconductor production equipment and a variety of industrial products.
China accounts for almost two-thirds of rare earth mining production and 92 per cent of global refined output, according to the International Energy Agency.

“It is true that exports of yttrium have stalled not only to Japan but worldwide, causing a supply-demand crunch and soaring prices,” a Japanese industry ministry official told AFP today, on condition of anonymity.
“Exports to Japan have decreased, including delays in shipments, and the global volume itself is low,” the official said.
The comments came after the Financial Times reported that Japan could exhaust its supply of the critical material in “months”.
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said in July that yttrium was “globally scarce” and was “an important rare earth for our country”.
According to Chinese customs data, exports of yttrium oxide to Japan amounted to 4,000 kilograms in September, compared with 51,000 kilograms in the same period the previous year.
The industry ministry official said Tokyo was working with the United States and European nations on critical mineral resources and rare earths, including yttrium.
Beijing has intensified pressure on Tokyo since Takaichi hinted last November that Japan could intervene militarily in any attack on self-ruled Taiwan.
China views Taiwan as its territory and has not ruled out taking it by force.

“China imposed export controls on Japan in accordance with laws and regulations, with the aim of curbing Japan’s attempts at remilitarisation and possessing nuclear weapons,” Chinese foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning told a regular briefing today.

Japan has asked the US government and American businesses to press China to ease rare earth export controls to avoid “severe disruption to the global automotive, defence and chip industries”, the Financial Times report said.
US defence supply chains rely on Japanese components that use yttrium, the newspaper said. — AFP
05c8eb78562a8d38: This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.
Introducing: the Impossible issue

We wanted our last print edition of 2026 to include a slate of stories that check in on impossible ideas. Why? Because it’s fun to dream about living on other planets or uploading our brains. But also because scientists and engineers who won’t give up on daring endeavors remind us what technology is supposed to do: make life better, safer, healthier, even more joyful.

That’s the ambition behind the stories in our new Impossible issue. We explore bold attempts to make synthetic blood, build cities on the moon, and attain cognitive immortality. We investigate AI’s ability to say no, a bionic eye that can restore sight, and high hopes for blended meat. Plus, we check in on six technologies that have been “coming soon” for years.
This issue is for the folks with the audacity to try, and refuse to let anyone—themselves included— tell them no. We hope you enjoy the ride.
Astrolab’s upcoming rover will run the first LLMs on the moon

Large language models are set to go lunar. A computer capable of running AI software is one of the payloads aboard Astrolab’s FLIP lunar rover, which is slated to head to the moon as early as next month.

The mission will test whether LLMs can enable greater autonomy and real-time intelligent decision-making in the extreme lunar environment. But the moon will present formidable challenges, from extreme temperatures to intense cosmic radiation.
Find out how the lunar rover could change the future of space exploration.
—Tereza Pultarova
How to study a swiftly melting climate disaster

In Alaska’s Denali National Park, a 2013 lightning fire burned nearly 35,000 acres, stripping away the insulating layer that preserves permafrost. It’s given scientists a rare opportunity to study how fires reshape permafrost and carbon storage over time.

The work is providing critical clues into the complex mechanisms driving cascading climate feedback effects. As warming temperatures fuel fires, more permafrost thaws, releasing greenhouse-gas emissions that threaten to fuel more warming, fires and permafrost loss. Their observations are revealing worrisome signs about what lies ahead.
Discover what their fieldwork is revealing about a cascading climate disaster.
—James Temple
MIT Technology Review Narrated: the explosive claim that’s upended the AI world

“I think I have good news about the nature of neural networks.” With those simple words of optimism, Nick Cammarata, a researcher at AI startup Goodfire, kicked off a 26,000-word blog post that has knocked the industry on its head.
Cammarata claims that LLMs might be far easier to understand, and thus to monitor and control, than people previously thought. If true, it’s a huge deal. But not everyone is convinced.

MIT Technology Review spoke to Cammarata the day after his post blew up. He explained what he thinks researchers are getting wrong, what his work actually shows, and why skeptics aren’t ready to celebrate just yet.

This is our latest story to become an MIT Technology Review Narrated podcast, which we publish each week on Spotify and Apple Podcasts. Just navigate to MIT Technology Review Narrated on either platform, and follow us to get all our new content as it’s released.

As Witkoff touched down in Putin's home city, Russia announced it would soon begin shipments of diesel to the United States under a deal with Trump and that it had freed a US citizen – Stephen Hubbard – held by Moscow since the start of the war on allegations of fighting as a "mercenary" for Ukraine.

"We've brought some papers. It's really some ideas, some sort of peace deal between Russia and Ukraine, and you'll read that at your leisure," Witkoff – Trump's business partner and envoy – told Putin in Saint Petersburg's Konstantinovsky Palace.
Putin thanked Trump for his efforts to resolve the war and said he was eager to be informed about the US meeting with Zelensky.
The long-time Russian leader has repeatedly refused to hold face-to-face talks with Zelensky and said that Moscow intends to seize the rest of eastern Ukraine.
Witkoff told Putin he hoped trilateral talks can resume.
"I'm hoping that you might consider that as a next step in the peace process so we can begin to have technical teams discussing what those next steps are," he told the Russian leader.
Putin thanked Trump for his "attention" to the conflict and said the US leader had "insisted that it was necessary to end this conflict" in their last phone call.
Russia's war against Ukraine has killed hundreds of thousands of troops on both sides as well as thousands of civilians.
As Witkoff arrived in Saint Petersburg, Kyiv said Moscow's strikes killed at least four people – including two in the capital and an elderly couple in the eastern Kharkiv region.
'Momentum' in talks
Meeting Putin, Witkoff described his talks with Zelensky as "productive".
"I think there's some degree of momentum, and I hope that today can be another step forward in the peace process and discussing how we resolve the Ukrainian conflict," he said.
Zelensky on Tuesday thanked Washington for the resumption of US intelligence sharing on Russian strikes.

The Witkoff-Zelensky meeting in Norway followed days of friction between Washington and Kyiv, with Zelensky urging the US not to side with Russia and Trump calling for the Ukrainian leader to be replaced.
Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner is also due to participate in Wednesday's talks with Putin remotely.
US-led talks on the conflict have so far not led to a breakthrough, and Moscow insists it intends to press on with its offensive.

Witkoff also told Putin that Washington was "grateful" for a diesel deal – met with astonishment in Kyiv and across Europe – that saw US sanctions on Moscow eased to allow Russian fuel to flow to the US.
The deal has been seen as a way to try to lower fuel prices for American consumers ahead of testing midterm elections in the US next month.
Washington was interested in further "business and economic cooperation" with Russia when the war ends, Witkoff said.
"We even talk about it now openly with the Ukrainians to give them some sort of sense about what the possibilities will be when this whole conflict is over," he said.
Kyiv has pleaded with Western countries to put more pressure on Moscow and not lift sanctions.
Ahead of the talks, Putin announced that Stephen Hubbard, an American taken captive by Russian forces in Ukraine in 2022 and later sentenced to almost seven years in prison, had been freed.
Trump had asked the Russian leader to free Hubbard, a retired English teacher in his 70s who had always denied the charges he was a "mercenary" fighting for Ukraine.
Witkoff hailed the move and called Putin a "humanitarian".
Trump later said that Hubbard was on his way to the Unites States and that the release had not been part of a swap deal.

c1694d54ef326451: When it comes to cyberattacks that shut down power grids, drinking-water systems, and other critical infrastructure, AI doesn’t – yet – turn script kiddies into sophisticated, nation-state attackers. But “the potential is there,” according to operational technology (OT) security experts.

"One thing that we've relied on for years is security by obscurity when it comes to utilities," said Steve Swick, former chief information security officer at American Electric Power. "The knowledge needed to do some of that stuff is getting less likely to be necessary," Swick added during a media panel ahead of the publication of Frenos' State of AI in Security report.
AI makes it easier and faster for human attackers to target critical infrastructure, gain access to utilities and manufacturing plants, and perform OT system reconnaissance.

“Basic access can recon documentation, and distill through that documentation very quickly to find out critical design features of your plant and facility,” said Paul Shaver, head of OT at Armadin, during the panel. “I can download the manual for almost any automation controller, parse through that very quickly, and come up with ways that I can exploit a dedicated feature of something that was not secure by design.”

Armadin is Kevin Mandia’s new security startup that uses swarms of autonomous AI agents to simulate real-world cyberattacks. Prior to joining Armadin, Shaver spent six years as the global OT practice leader at Mandia’s earlier company, Mandiant, which Google acquired in 2022.

“I will fly my Mandiant flag for a second and try to steer away from the fear, uncertainty, and death of the world is coming to an end, and every script kiddie is now a very sophisticated nation-state adversary. But I’m not going to say the potential is not there, because the tools are improving such that the access to information is so much quicker.”

At Armadin, and with an AI assist, “I'm very quickly building tools in days that would normally have taken me months,” Shaver said. “If it can do that for me, it's doing something similar for the folks that have a very basic skill set. I wouldn't go so far as to script kiddies yet, but as the models improve, that becomes more of a possibility in this space.”

Plus, as AI lowers the technical barriers to would-be OT hackers, “it advances the timeline,” said Harry Thomas, chief technology officer and co-founder of Frenos, a security company that does AI pentesting for OT environments.

“If a better-than-average script kiddie can now perform attacks,” Thomas said, “You have more threat actors out there. There's an acceleration in timeline, more attacks could be happening, and from a defensive position, you might not know who your threat actor is anymore.”
Testing the power of LLMs to help plan attacks

The Frenos report, published Wednesday, examined the extent to which AI could help someone plan an attack on industrial systems. To do this, it ran several AI models through 16,980 tests between October 2025 and September 2026. These included 13,884 decision attempts, 2,520 planning attempts, and 576 simulated attacks.

The company won’t disclose the models or providers’ names, but said it tested six frontier models, two US open weight models, and two foreign open weight models, on three kinds of tasks: choosing one action, planning the steps to a goal, and working through a simulated scenario.

Each test gave the model background information and a set of attack actions to choose from. Before choosing, each model received details about assets, networks, and known weaknesses, plus the access each action required.
Frenos then checked whether the model’s choice matched the required outcome. Depending on the model, between 6 percent and 47 percent of the choices passed.

These tests found that the strongest three frontier models succeeded in about 90 percent of their planning attempts – meaning they produced a workable attack plan – but these same models weren’t consistent: 60 percent, 62.9 percent, and 74.3 percent of the attack plans passed every repeat.

“A plan can look sensible and still leave out something essential,” according to the report. “The models had information about the task, but some answers skipped a step or assumed access that the plan had not established.”

Meanwhile, the most successful of the four open weight models – a non-US model – achieved a 36.2 percent overall success rate. That figure, however, was still higher than the overall success rates of three other US frontier models, which scored 31.9 percent, 18.8 percent, and 17.9 percent, respectively.

“We're seeing that even though AI models help us accelerate our tooling, accelerate our access and knowledge transfer, they are still prone to hallucinations – aka mistakes,” Thomas said. “We still think human judgment remains essential for these AI models to make the threat actors achieve whatever mission or goal they're trying to achieve.”

In these tests, no humans asked the models to correct their plans, whereas in a real-life attack, a miscreant who understood the target could spot a gap in the AI’s plan, provide more information, and ask the model to revise its answer.

“On top of that, when we were testing the AI models, we used a harness that was pretty simple: Here's some information. Here's the context. Give me an answer,” Thomas said. “A more capable harness could have given these AI models more of an edge.”

Based on the findings, Frenos recommends actions for OT defenders to take, starting with a layered defense. This involves segmenting networks, limiting remote access and user permissions, and testing recovery steps.
“We have our business continuity plans and disaster recovery plans for a reason,” Thomas said. “Let's execute them.” ®

00989dfdfa2c8d0d: PARIS: President Emmanuel Macron on Wednesday took an apparent swipe at counterpart Donald Trump of exploiting France's riots for advantage in the US midterm election battle, as Paris prepared for more protests this weekend.

Macron, speaking during a visit to Qatar, implied that Trump, and possibly Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who is also in election mode, made "stupid comments" on the unrest for political gain, though he did not name either leader.
"There are people who campaign at France's expense – leaders who are in campaign mode, whether here in the region or on the other side of the Atlantic," he told reporters in Doha.

Macron made his remarks as he and his government struggled to get on top of a crisis that has scarred France's image both abroad and in financial markets, six months ahead of presidential elections to choose his successor.
France's government has admitted it "lost control" in the frenzy of street violence that erupted last weekend, when masked youths clashed with police, looted shops and vandalised public buildings.
Trump has sought to link the "revolution" in France to "migrants, jihadists, and communists" as he campaigned for his Republican party in the United States on his anti-immigration messaging.
He also on Tuesday hailed French far-right leader Marine Le Pen, who shares his ideologies, as a conservative voice, with surveys putting her as the frontrunner in France's presidential race.
Trump's ally Netanyahu, facing his own tough election battle, on Tuesday argued that France had been hit by an "invasion."
Several analysts have dismissed the claims that migrants were driving France's protests.
- CURFEWS -

The unrest overshadowed demonstrations held Saturday in which more than half a million people marched nationwide against the cost of living. Those rallies followed four weeks of student protests that have closed many schools across France.
Since the rioting – the worst France has seen in years – and ahead of further cost-of-living demonstrations this coming Saturday, Macron's government has warned it will brook no further violence.
Authorities in Paris and several other cities imposed nighttime curfews Monday and Tuesday in certain zones prone to protests or looting.
Macron said that on Thursday he would chair a meeting of key ministers and intelligence officials to receive a "detailed account" of what happened last weekend.

French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu, who on Wednesday held a meeting with union leaders organising marches, has vowed a "massive" police deployment for the fresh demonstrations called for Saturday by the Yellow Vest movement protesting rising inflation.
The convulsion in France, the EU's second-biggest economy after Germany, has rattled financial markets already nervous about the country's growing debt pile and deficit.

The yield on the French government's benchmark 10-year bond has been rising, and on Wednesday surpassed five percent as investors demanded a higher return given the fiscal woes. A rising yield signifies a drop in bond prices. The Paris stock market also fell.
On Friday, the Moody's ratings agency is expected to lower its grade on France's public debt.

The country's political landscape is so fragmented that Lecornu has little chance of winning swift parliamentary consensus for a cost-cutting budget that needs to be adopted before the end of this year.
- LE PEN LEADS RACE -

The latest survey, carried out by Ifop in the wake of the riots, suggested Le Pen would lead first-round voting intentions by a wide margin and far-left candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon emerged as her most likely opponent in the runoff.
France's neighbours Italy and Belgium have also started to experience similar unrest, on a smaller scale. Italy's government has ordered 500 troops to Milan to stem street violence there.

Macron said that "we don't need a state of emergency" that would likewise permit soldiers to reinforce police against rioters, adding that "we have the means" already at authorities' disposal, such as curfews.
While the partial curfews have led to a calming of the situation in Paris and elsewhere, they have disrupted travel for commuters looking to take urban rail after 11pm (2100 GMT).

"It's quite disconcerting," said one Paris commuter who gave only his first name, Louis, when he found his line closed. But "if it can prevent further acts of vandalism... then yes, I think it's a good thing", he said.
The Yellow Vest movement behind last weekend's demonstrations announced Wednesday it had formally told authorities it planned to hold its Paris march on Saturday starting from Bastille square.
The movement also wants to hold follow-up nationwide demonstrations on Nov 5.

The images broadcast around the world of France's street violence last weekend have prompted several countries, including the United States, China and Germany, to issue travel advisories for their citizens in France.--AFP

c66cd96b194bb521: JAKARTA, Oct 21 — Indonesia’s president lashed out at MSCI today, accusing the index compiler of “trying to scare us” over its threat to downgrade the country’s stock market.
MSCI said last week it was “no longer appropriate” to classify Indonesia as an emerging market, citing investor concerns over shareholding structures and trading behaviour.
The benchmark Jakarta Composite Index (JCI) then plunged more than 11 per cent on Friday — its biggest single-day fall since 1998 — on fears of an exodus of foreign investment.
Addressing his cabinet today, Prabowo Subianto said: “We continue to be confronted by all kinds of things, MSCI, all sorts of things, trying to scare us.
“I only say this to MSCI: the Indonesian nation is not afraid of anyone and will not be intimidated.”
The JCI closed 0.94 per cent higher today, having sunk earlier in the week to its lowest level since late 2020.
It has plummeted more than 40 per cent since the start of the year, placing it among the world’s worst-performing indexes.
The MSCI has cited investor concerns over “ongoing opacity in shareholding structures” as well as coordinated trading behaviour that has affected price information.
It is considering reclassifying Indonesia as a “standalone market”, which could force investment funds tracking the MSCI’s emerging market indexes to sell Indonesian holdings.
On Monday, Indonesia Stock Exchange (IDX) boss Jeffrey Hendrik announced measures to improve market transparency, including publicly providing more information on small shareholders.
The IDX would also remove “all shares with high shareholding concentration from the composite stock price index” to provide a more reasonable picture of JCI movements.
Indonesia’s economy has been hit hard by surging fuel prices due to the Middle East war.
The country of 287 million people is a net oil importer, but the government has insisted on leaving heavily subsidised fuel prices unchanged, despite struggling with high costs.
As food and commodities prices have risen, albeit within the target range, the economic strain has triggered protests, and Prabowo’s ratings are at a record low.
Today he said the country faced “many” difficulties and disruptions.
“We are not afraid. We have strength, we have courage, and we are willing to make sacrifices,” Prabowo said.
“We do not know the meaning of surrender... If necessary, we will carry out massive savings. We will be even more thrifty later on.”
Indonesia’s central bank today kept its key lending rate steady at 5.75 per cent after three hikes so far this year. — AFP

f1c451535c174654: KOTA KINABALU: A group of Kadazan-Dusun villagers in Kota Marudu is fighting a bid by the Sabah and federal governments to strike out a lawsuit over alleged neglect and their ancestral land rights without a trial.

The villagers, represented by Amli Nohin, Jaikon Majumban and Jaripi Ompok, claim that they have been deprived of basic amenities, including roads, electricity, clean water, accessible healthcare, schooling, and reliable mobile coverage.
They also seek recognition of their native customary rights over ancestral land within the Lingkabau Forest Reserve.
In a submission filed last week, the villagers argued that their claims raised serious legal and constitutional questions that should be decided after a full trial.
The High Court in Kota Kinabalu heard the parties today and will deliver its decision on Dec 9 on the state's application to strike out the suit.

According to their statement, residents of Kampung Sonsogon Makatol Darat must walk about five hours through rough terrain to reach the nearest road, while the nearest government clinic is about eight hours away.
Medical assistance depends on helicopter visits by mobile teams, which are sometimes cancelled because of bad weather.
The villagers also claim that children must live at school premises, away from their families, to attend classes.
On the land dispute, they allege that the state granted a permit to Azam Surianiaga Sdn Bhd in May 2023 without consulting or compensating the community.
The state denies the claims, arguing that the government owes no enforceable duty to provide the specific level of public services sought.
It also says development spending is a policy matter and that native land claims must follow procedures under the Sabah Land Ordinance.

The villagers contend that the state cannot rely on procedures that were not used before the permit was granted. They also cite court decisions recognising fiduciary duties towards indigenous communities over customary land.
Their lawyer, Amli, said the villagers were asking the court to decide whether their legal and constitutional rights have been infringed.
"A remote native community deserves its day in court on full evidence, not a summary dismissal," he said.

French prime minister Sebastien Lecornu, who on Wednesday held a meeting with union leaders organising marches, has vowed a "massive" police deployment for the fresh demonstrations called for Saturday by the Yellow Vest movement protesting rising inflation.
The convulsion in France, the EU's second-biggest economy after Germany, has rattled financial markets already nervous about the country's growing debt pile and deficit.

The yield on the French government's benchmark 10-year bond has been rising and on Wednesday surpassed five percent as investors demanded a higher return given the fiscal woes. A rising yield signifies a drop in bond prices. The Paris stock market also fell.
On Friday, the Moody's ratings agency is expected to lower its grade on France's public debt.

The country's political landscape is so fragmented that Lecornu has little chance of winning swift parliamentary consensus for a cost-cutting budget that needs to be adopted before the end of this year.
Le Pen leads race

The latest survey, carried out by Ifop in the wake of the riots, suggested Le Pen would lead first-round voting intentions by a wide margin, and far-left candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon emerged as her most likely opponent in the runoff.
France's neighbours Italy and Belgium have also started to experience similar unrest, on a smaller scale. Italy's government has ordered 500 troops to Milan to stem street violence there.

Macron said that "we don't need a state of emergency" that would likewise permit soldiers to reinforce police against rioters, adding that "we have the means" already at authorities' disposal, such as curfews.
While the partial curfews have led to a calming of the situation in Paris and elsewhere, they have disrupted travel for commuters looking to take urban rail after 11.00pm (2100 GMT).

"It's quite disconcerting," said one Paris commuter who gave only his first name, Louis, when he found his line closed. But "if it can prevent further acts of vandalism... then yes, I think it's a good thing", he said.
The Yellow Vest movement behind last weekend's demonstrations announced Wednesday it had formally told authorities it planned to hold its Paris march on Saturday starting from Bastille Square.
The movement also wants to hold follow-up nationwide demonstrations on Nov 5.

The images broadcast around the world of France's street violence last weekend have prompted several countries, including the United States, China and Germany, to issue travel advisories for their citizens in France.
a9b74b59016f0a72: BERLIN, Oct 21 — Sebastian Vettel has revealed that his first contact with Ferrari came after his second Formula One world title, but he turned the Scuderia down at the time because he was happy and successful at Red Bull, reported German Press Agency (dpa).
“The first contact came in 2012 after the second title,” Vettel said in a documentary about him by public broadcaster ARD, titled Being Sebastian Vettel.
Vettel said he received a letter from then Ferrari president Luca di Montezemolo congratulating him, “without referring to anything else”.
But Ferrari, looking to return to the winning ways it had enjoyed a few years earlier during the Michael Schumacher era, went a step further.
Vettel said he had “a very secret meeting” with Di Montezemolo, during which “he asked, what is the contractual situation, do you want to drive for Ferrari?”
Vettel said he saw no reason to move at the time.
“So I turned them down, but of course I left the door open a little bit,” he said.
Vettel won two more world titles with Red Bull in 2012 and 2013, but eventually joined Ferrari in 2015 after a winless final season with the team.
He won 14 races for the Scuderia out of 53 victories in his Formula One career, but failed to secure a world title with Ferrari.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Aston Martin’s German driver Sebastian Vettel attends a presser ahead of the Abu Dhabi Formula One Grand Prix at the Yas Marina Circuit in the Emirati city of Abu Dhabi November 17, 2022. — AFP pic
He left the team after the 2020 season and retired in 2022 following two seasons with Aston Martin.
The four-part documentary, available from tomorrow, also explores the sacrifices his parents made to finance his racing career in its early days.

“Of course I was aware that the financial situation was tense, that it wasn’t easy when the next reminder notice arrived at home,” Vettel said, adding that he had felt a responsibility to deliver from his early karting days onwards.
Vettel became the youngest world champion at the age of 23 in 2010.
However, he is set to lose that record to Mercedes driver Kimi Antonelli, who is 20 and has his first chance to clinch the 2026 title on Sunday at the United States (US) Grand Prix.
Others appearing in the documentary include Vettel’s former Red Bull mentor Helmut Marko and Lewis Hamilton, his long-time rival who became a friend.
Like Vettel, Hamilton has interests beyond motorsport.
Vettel also discusses former German economy minister Robert Habeck of the Green Party, reflecting his engagement with environmental protection and sustainability.
The documentary opens with Vettel holding a non-F1 trophy — a glass rhinoceros he received after being named Environmentalist of the Year in early 2026.
“I believe that the path I have now begun to follow is sustainable in the sense that it brings me fulfilment,” Vettel said. — Bernama-dpa
a6cc3f2b37961371: PUTRAJAYA: Mahkamah Rayuan membenarkan sebahagian rayuan Badan Peguam berhubung perarakan 'Walk for Judicial Independence' pada 2022, dan memberikan ganti rugi berjumlah RM59,499 susulan pelanggaran hak mereka di bawah Perlembagaan.

Sidang tiga hakim diketuai Choo Kah Sing memerintahkan kerajaan membayar ganti rugi khas sebanyak RM19,499 kepada Badan Peguam, serta RM10,000 kepada Karen Cheah Yee Lynn, Ezri Abdul Wahab, B Anand Raj dan Murshidah Mustafa, yang memegang jawatan dalam organisasi itu ketika saman difailkan.

Perarakan itu dianjurkan pada 17 Jun 2022 bagi membantah pengumuman Suruhanjaya Pencegahan Rasuah Malaysia mengenai siasatan terhadap Hakim Nazlan Ghazali, ketika itu di Mahkamah Rayuan dan kini Mahkamah Persekutuan.
Badan Peguam menyifatkan pengumuman itu sebagai campur tangan terhadap kebebasan kehakiman dan pelanggaran prinsip pengasingan kuasa.
Pada 20 Mac tahun lepas, Mahkamah Tinggi memutuskan bahawa polis bertindak ultra vires, atau melampaui bidang kuasa, dengan mengenakan syarat yang melarang perarakan itu.
Bagaimanapun, mahkamah hanya memberikan ganti rugi nominal sebanyak RM1 kepada Badan Peguam, jumlah yang dicadangkan oleh peguam yang mewakili organisasi itu.

Saman itu difailkan pada 20 Okt 2022 terhadap enam defendan termasuk bekas ketua polis Dang Wangi iaitu Noor Dellhan Yahaya, ketua polis negara, menteri dalam negeri dan kerajaan Malaysia berhubung dakwaan pelanggaran hak plaintif di bawah Akta Perhimpunan Aman.

Menerusi pernyataan tuntutan, plaintif mendakwa semua defendan melanggar hak mereka di bawah akta berkenaan dengan melarang plaintif dan 500 ahli serta pelatih masing-masing daripada mengadakan perhimpunan di tempat letak kereta Padang Merbok, Jalan Parlimen ke pintu masuk utama bangunan Parlimen pada 17 Jun 2022 untuk menyerahkan memorandum kepada perdana menteri ketika itu, Ismail Sabri Yaakob, atau wakil beliau.

Ketika menyampaikan penghakiman, Choo yang bersidang bersama-sama Faizah Jamaludin dan Lim Hock Leng turut mengetepikan dapatan Mahkamah Tinggi bahawa kebenaran Dewan Bandaraya Kuala Lumpur diperlukan bagi mengadakan perhimpunan di Padang Merbok.
Mahkamah memutuskan bahawa notis yang dikemukakan oleh Badan Peguam kepada polis di bawah Seksyen 9 Akta Perhimpunan Aman adalah sah.
"Surat daripada ketua polis Dang Wangi yang mengenakan syarat terhadap perarakan itu telah dikeluarkan selepas tamat tempoh yang ditetapkan dan oleh itu, adalah tidak sah.

"Badan Peguam telah memaklumkan kepada polis pada 3 Jun 2022 namun hanya menerima maklum balas pada 16 Jun, iaitu kurang daripada 24 jam sebelum perarakan itu. Di bawah Seksyen 14 Akta berkenaan, polis perlu memberikan maklum balas berserta sebarang syarat dalam tempoh tiga hari," katanya.
Bagaimanapun, sidang mengekalkan keputusan Mahkamah Tinggi yang menolak tuntutan berhubung pemenjaraan salah, mendapati bahawa kebebasan para peserta tidak disekat sepenuhnya.
"Walaupun para peserta dilarang berarak ke Bangunan Parlimen, mereka tidak dihalang secara fizikal daripada meninggalkan kawasan tersebut," katanya.

Mahkamah juga mengekalkan dapatan bahawa polis tidak bertanggungjawab atas salah laku dalam jawatan awam serta menolak tuntutan berkaitan isu itu memandangkan ia gagal memenuhi prasyarat subjektif yang tinggi sebagaimana dikehendaki undang-undang.
Selain itu, mahkamah memutuskan untuk tidak memberikan ganti rugi am, ganti rugi teruk atau ganti rugi teladan.

Mahkamah juga memerintahkan agar faedah pada kadar 5% setahun dikenakan ke atas jumlah ganti rugi yang diberikan bermula dari tarikh penghakiman Mahkamah Tinggi hingga penyelesaian penuh dan tiada perintah berhubung kos.

Plaintif menuntut ganti rugi khas berjumlah RM19,449, ganti rugi am, teruk dan teladan serta kos selain deklarasi bahawa hak-hak mereka dilanggar manakala penahanan mereka adalah salah dan tidak sah di sisi undang-undang.
